# ADR-001 — Country routing and published content

**Status** Human approved on 2026-11-22 ([approval record](../approvals/US-01-architecture-approval.md))  
**Applies to** US-01, with shared boundaries for US-02 and US-03  
**Basis** [US-01 Draft 3](../../spec/US-01.md), [specification approval](../approvals/US-01-spec-approval.md), assessment pp. 1–3 and 6–9

## Context

One Angular build serves Colombia and Chile. Editors publish independent country configuration in Strapi. The URL identifies the active country, including on reload and browser Back or Forward. The frontend needs published content and all customer and quote data stays in the browser.

## Proposed decision

- Use one client-rendered Angular application and one standalone Router tree. Serve the country selector at `/` and recognize `/:country/quote/details` for US-01. Reserve `plans` and `summary` children for the later steps. An explicit in-country entry route may link to Details. Unsupported country segments show the recoverable country-selection screen and retain the attempted URL. Accept exact uppercase `CO` and `CL` and replace the history entry with the lowercase canonical path for the same country. Other case variants remain unsupported. SPA navigation fallback applies to app paths, with API paths and asset requests kept separate.
- Decode the current Router parameter to `co | cl` before accessing content or quote state. React to parameter changes even when the Router reuses the component. Same-country wizard navigation can reuse its last valid, in-memory configuration. Initial load, page reload, country transition (including return to a previously visited country), and explicit retry require a new request. Clear ready status at refresh start. Cancel superseded reads and check both country and request generation before committing a response. A late or failed response leaves quote data intact and never renders as current. The URL carries the country and step only.
- Use a Strapi country enum, Draft & Publish, and one **Form Configuration collection document per country**, containing the complete field list as repeatable components. Each field inherits country from its owning form. This makes punctuation, copy, additions and removals, ordering, and option or validation edits one publishable snapshot. Editors use Content Manager for entries and may stage drafts without changing the live form. The serving controller reads published documents explicitly and treats multiple published form documents for one country as invalid rather than picking a winner. Seed by country without clobbering subsequent editorial changes. A stable editorial field key is distinct from Strapi's internal component IDs. [Strapi Document Service publication status](https://docs.strapi.io/cms/api/document-service/status)
- US-02 can use a separate Plan collection filtered by requested country, published status, and active flag, with stable plan identifiers, ordered plans, stored price/currency, coverages, benefits, and a recommended flag. US-03 can use a separate country Terms document with published text and a revision identifier. Their precise shapes, prices, and publication/acceptance rules belong to their future specifications. Changes to plans or terms need only their own publication.

## Public read boundary

The browser uses a same-origin `GET /api/quote-content/v1/:country/form` routed to Strapi through the static app host. Keep Strapi's ordinary Content API authorization enabled and grant the Public role the single custom `api::quote-content.quote-content.readForm` action. Enable neither generated CRUD routes for these content types nor public draft, preview, plugin, search, media, or admin actions. The frontend sends no authorization token. The static host proxies the dedicated read path only and returns no substitute SPA HTML for unmatched API paths. Admin access is a separate local binding and uses Strapi admin authentication for editorial access. [Strapi routing](https://docs.strapi.io/cms/backend-customization/routes), [Users & Permissions](https://docs.strapi.io/cms/features/users-permissions)

The controller takes the canonical country path parameter and no caller-controlled filters, locale, population, or publication selectors. It explicitly queries published data, populates only the known components, validates the whole content projection, and maps an allowlisted DTO. Success is `200` with `{ schemaVersion: 1, country, fields }` (see [ADR-002](ADR-002-dynamic-form-contract.md)). Public outcomes are `400 INVALID_REQUEST` for unsupported query inputs, `404 UNSUPPORTED_COUNTRY` for an unsupported API path code, `404 FORM_NOT_PUBLISHED` for no published document, `503 FORM_UNAVAILABLE` for configuration invalidity or duplicate documents, and `503 CONTENT_UNAVAILABLE` for CMS retrieval failure. A published document with no fields is invalid. Use a stable `{ error: { code } }` response without stack traces, internal IDs, or raw data. Use `Cache-Control: no-store` on these responses and bypass intermediary cache for this API path. The frontend still decodes success bodies and rejects country or version mismatches. Errors use local accessible fallback copy and retry. Future plan and terms routes require separate public actions after those stories' approvals.

## Alternatives and consequences

| Alternative | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| URL query, cookies, or geolocation | A query is shareable but easier to drop between steps. Device-derived defaults conflict with explicit URL country selection. |
| One frontend per market or per-locale builds | Independent releases could isolate releases, at the cost of duplicate deployment and violating the single-build requirement. |
| Strapi i18n as the country axis | Convenient for translations of shared records. Country controls eligibility, currency, and fields as well as language, so a country enum models the business boundary directly. |
| One Strapi record per field with public collection reads | Easier independent field editing, with more fragmented publication, larger permission surface, and more coupling to Strapi's REST shape. |
| An authenticated BFF with a server-side Strapi token | Supports private content at the cost of additional runtime and secret management. The proposed custom Strapi route already serves a narrow public projection. |

The custom route and decoder are deliberate maintenance costs. Editors can publish changes within the supported versioned vocabulary. New field primitives and incompatible contract changes are engineering changes. Confirm exact Public action registration and route permissions in the pinned Strapi version during implementation before exposing the route. Verify both canonical URLs after a hard reload, draft exclusion, rejection of cross-country responses and query overrides, denial of anonymous writes and generated reads, and published change pickup without rebuilding Angular. Trace to AC-US01-01, 05, 08, 09, 11 and 13 and T-US01-01, 06, 08, 09, 11 and 13.

[Angular route state](https://angular.dev/guide/routing/read-route-state), [Angular deep-link deployment](https://angular.dev/tools/cli/deployment)
# ADR-002 — Typed dynamic form contract and reconciliation

**Status** Human approved on 2026-11-22 ([approval record](../approvals/US-01-architecture-approval.md))  
**Applies to** US-01, with stable fields and roles for US-02 and US-03  
**Basis** [US-01 Draft 3](../../spec/US-01.md), especially AC-US01-02–04, 07–10 and 12–16, and [ADR-001](ADR-001-multi-country-content.md)

## Context

Strapi editors need to change field content and validation without rebuilding Angular. The application must reject a bad configuration atomically, preserve a compatible draft across changes, and display one configured error per field. A dynamic CMS key cannot provide static knowledge of its eventual widget or value type.

## Proposed decision

### Contract and failure behavior

Decode `unknown` once at each trust boundary using framework-independent TypeScript guards that produce a discriminated `FieldDefinition` union. A small shared workspace contract can supply the decoder, pure validation and fixtures to Strapi's projection and Angular's consumer. It carries no Angular or Strapi dependency and no customer data. Keep Strapi's nested editor representation behind its explicit projection. Contract version 1 is a fixed envelope with an exact version, the requested canonical country, and a nonempty fields array. Render content strings as text, including labels, help and errors. Each field has the following projected properties.

| Property | Version 1 proposal |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `label`, `helpText`, `errorMessage` | Stable editor-maintained ID unique within the country form, Spanish label and fallback field error, and a required help-text property that permits an empty string. IDs are restricted opaque strings, protected from reserved object keys and independent of labels, order, and Strapi component IDs. |
| `kind`, `required`, `order` | One supported kind, a Boolean required flag, and a nonnegative safe-integer order. Sort by order, then by ID on a tie. Country is inherited from the form. |
| `rules` | Ordered array, possibly empty. Each rule specifies a recognized operator, its typed arguments when relevant, and its configured Spanish message. Order is the editor's array order. |
| `options`, `defaultValue` | Options are permitted only on selects and require stable unique option IDs and nonempty labels within each select. An omitted default means unset. A present default must meet the field's representation, available options, and configured rules. Fresh required selects start unset, so publishing a default for one is invalid. |
| `purpose` | Optional semantic marker, unique per reserved role. A usable form contains one required `dateOfBirth` date with `minimumAge` 18 and one required `vehicleYear` number with `vehicleYearRange`. `identityDocument` and `licensePlate` markers, when present, use text fields. This enables masking and pricing without relying on visible labels. |

Reject missing mandatory properties, missing published fields, date or number representation errors in rule arguments, incompatible defaults, unknown types or operators, duplicate IDs, and required selects with no valid options. Validate each option. An invalid option definition fails the snapshot. Allow an optional select to have no options and remain unset. Reject inverted range endpoints and a duplicate required rule. A rejected refresh never partially updates the view or the stored draft. Apply the error and retry behavior in ADR-001. Enforce size limits on fields, options, and text at the contract boundary. Choose exact limits during implementation against fixtures and document them.

### Type and rule compatibility

| Kinds and values | Supported operators |
| --- | --- |
| Text, a string, including document numbers and plates | `required`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern`, `email` |
| Number, a finite JavaScript number | `required`, `min`, `max`, `vehicleYearRange` for the vehicle-year purpose |
| Select, a listed stable option ID string | `required` |
| Date, a valid Gregorian ISO calendar-date string `YYYY-MM-DD` | `required`, `minDate`, `maxDate`, `minimumAge` for the date-of-birth purpose |
| Checkbox, a Boolean | `required`, which requires explicit `true` for a required checkbox |

- Keep a single required check. The field flag controls requiredness. An optional explicit `required` rule is valid only when the flag is true and supplies the required message. A required flag without the rule uses the field's configured error message. Required checks distinguish missing values from numeric zero. Whitespace-only text is empty for the required check and stored document or plate strings retain leading zeros. Non-required rules treat an unset value as inapplicable. An invalid typed entry is distinct from an unset value. Apply validators to every field and retain the ordered outcomes. The required error wins when present, then the first failing configured rule, then the field fallback for an invalid representation no configured rule describes.
- Length and age arguments are nonnegative integers, and lengths count Unicode code points. Numeric bounds are finite and inclusive. Vehicle year requires a safe integer and uses local browser Gregorian year Y with inclusive Y−20 through Y+1. Date bounds are valid ISO dates and inclusive. Calculate age using Gregorian calendar components and the browser's local civil date via an injectable clock, avoiding UTC parsing shifts. Propose March 1 for a February 29 birthday in non-leap years in the simulator. `required`, `email`, and `vehicleYearRange` take no argument.
- Treat patterns as declarative whole-value checks in a bounded safe subset. Propose bounded character classes, literal segments, and bounded repetitions, with no backreferences, lookaround, groups, or unbounded repetition. Cap both pattern and input lengths. Use a bounded non-backtracking matcher for the subset or equivalent implementation whose cost is bounded on rejected input. Validate editor patterns before the config reaches ready state. This makes formatting changes publishable while keeping pattern matching predictable.

### Angular form and accessibility

Use Typed Reactive Forms with `FormRecord<FormControl<FieldValue | null>>` and a discriminated field/view model. Keys are dynamic and the control's static value type is the common union. Narrow by the decoded field kind and normalize at the control adapter and output boundaries. Use actual typed number and Boolean values, preserve meaningful empty or unset state, and track rendered elements by stable ID. Stay with native inputs and selects and an unset, non-selectable required-select placeholder. The first invalid field gets focus on an unsuccessful Continue. Keep Continue available after the configuration is ready, with application validation controlling progress and custom messages. Use native form semantics with an explicit Angular submit handler and no browser validation bubbles masking configured messages. On blur expose that field's message, on change reevaluate touched fields, and on submit expose all applicable errors. Associate visible errors and help through stable DOM IDs and `aria-describedby`, and set `aria-invalid` when showing an error. Use concise status announcements for loading and retry, and avoid announcing the same validation error twice when moving focus. [Angular typed forms](https://angular.dev/guide/forms/typed-forms)

### Deterministic reconciliation

Rebuild the draft from the latest valid fields by ID instead of mutating the old key map in place. Omit removed or replaced IDs and obsolete select options entirely. For new IDs apply a valid allowed default or leave unset. For existing IDs preserve representable values and keep label, help, and order edits independent, even if updated business rules make a preserved value invalid. This lets users correct a value after a stricter constraint is published. Check the previous kind as well as the primitive value. Preserve a date as text, or text as a date only when it is already a valid ISO date. Clear other kind changes without implicit coercion. Select values require membership in the new option IDs and never migrate by label. Revalidate every field against the current clock and refreshed rules, write the clean snapshot atomically, and gate progression on the result. A restored valid required select stays selected. A fresh one, or one with an obsolete selection, shows its placeholder.

## Alternatives and consequences

| Alternative | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| Hardcoded Angular fields or a FormGroup with fixed keys | Strong static key typing, with a code change for each CMS field change. |
| Untyped forms or a general JSON Schema rendering engine | Simpler generalization, with weaker app-level typing or an extra dependency and a harder-to-explain CMS contract. |
| Signal Forms | Fits a signal-first model and is stable in Angular 22. The proposed Angular 21 baseline and requested form preference favor Typed Reactive Forms. Signals still own non-control state. |
| Directly execute CMS regexes or arbitrary editor rules | Broader flexibility, with less predictable runtime cost and harder validation of whole snapshots. |

The proposal makes unsupported widgets and rule language changes schema work. It protects the required age and year invariants while permitting published changes to supported field content. The type matrix, safe pattern subset, date boundary convention, and required-select default restriction are proposed architecture decisions. Verify DTO acceptance and rejection in both consumers, age and year boundaries, required-first and rule order, data reconciliation, stale response rejection, keyboard focus, and the two required-select states. See T-US01-02–06, 08–10, 12 and 14–16. The final quote-summary view remains under US-03.
# ADR-003 — Frontend-only wizard state

**Status** Human approved on 2026-11-22 ([approval record](../approvals/US-01-architecture-approval.md))  
**Applies to** US-01, with shared state boundaries for US-02 and US-03  
**Basis** [US-01 Draft 3](../../spec/US-01.md), assessment pp. 2 and 6–9, and project owner's frontend-only data boundary

## Context

Step 1 must restore a draft when navigating back and reconcile from a newly retrieved form. Later steps depend on the same vehicle and policyholder data, plan selection, and terms and simulated payment status. Strapi owns business content. It does not receive customer, vehicle, quote, plan selection, or payment data.

## Proposed decision

Use a small Angular Signals store with explicit commands, typed snapshots, and read-only projections. Scope it to the app's quoting flow so route components can be recreated. Pass the country's decoded Router value to state accessors and store separate country snapshots. Never read a previous country's data while a new country is loading. Store normalized typed drafts with original field kind and stable field identifier; keep touch/submit and focus state in the component. The reconciler atomically replaces the active snapshot after a valid refresh and the store supplies the later-step projection only for the active country.

Use a small versioned, tab-scoped `sessionStorage` envelope for fictitious wizard state. The signal store owns the current state; the adapter writes full snapshots and validates the restored shape and country. Treat browser storage as untrusted, revalidate fields against freshly retrieved content before advancing, and reject malformed or unknown-version stored data. A recoverable content error retains the draft but blocks progression. If storage is blocked or fails, continue using memory for the current page session and make reload recovery unavailable. Clear the country draft when the user starts a new quote. Do not put quote data in URLs, cookies, analytics, diagnostic logs, content requests, or server persistence. App-opened separate tabs should omit `opener` where relevant. A duplicated or opener-linked tab can inherit an initial copy and then diverge. The design promises no cross-tab or cross-device guarantees. [HTML Web Storage standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webstorage.html)

The US-01 step-2 handoff can be verified with a same-country route or narrow screen that allows going back. It owns no plan UI or plan business behavior. Future deep links to plans or summary check the matching country and current prerequisites, then navigate to the earliest incomplete step within that country. Client guards are wizard navigation controls. The data boundary is implemented by the public API shape and the absence of quote-write operations. [Angular Router guards](https://angular.dev/guide/routing/route-guards)

## Consequences for later stories

- **US-02** consumes a current, validated Step 1 snapshot and published active country plans. Store only one selected plan reference per quote along with the calculated price snapshot and its inputs or revision linkage as specified later. A change to inputs or available plans invalidates dependent selections or totals when the later rules require it. Recheck prerequisites before summary.
- **US-03** derives the review from current country fields and masks the identity document in presentation. Use stable field purpose metadata to locate the document independently of its label. Bind consent to the current terms revision and quote snapshot. Proposed duplicate protection is an atomic attempt transition in the same store, from eligible to processing before the asynchronous simulation starts. Only the matching attempt can settle, repeat clicks do not enqueue, success keeps one confirmation number for that completed quote, and a reported failure may retry. The US-03 spec and checkpoint will decide how reload handles a persisted processing attempt and completed receipt. No real gateway, card data or global idempotency service is implied.

## Alternatives and consequences

| Alternative | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| Memory only | Lowest retention, with loss on reload and no reconciliation of previously saved data after refresh. |
| Browser persistent storage or IndexedDB | Longer recovery and broader synchronization options, with unnecessary fictitious customer-data retention and more cleanup or coordination. |
| Server quote collection or hosted state | Could support cross-device resume and global deduplication, contrary to the frontend-only customer and quote data boundary. |
| General-purpose state management library | Provides conventions for large applications. Three wizard steps can share a signal store without that dependency. |

Verify same-country Back and Forward, country-switch isolation, restoration plus reconciliation after reload, graceful storage failure, and exclusion of quote data from network requests. Exercise duplicate payment attempts and reload outcomes under US-03. US-01 traces to AC-US01-06, 08, 09, 13 and 14 and T-US01-07, 08, 09, 13 and 14.

# US-02 — Plan List

**Status:** Draft 1 · Human approved  
**Source:** `requirements/technical-assessment.pdf`, pages 2–3 and 7  
**Related story:** US-02 — Plan list  
**Dependencies:** Approved US-01 and ADR-001, ADR-002, ADR-003

## Objective

As a person getting a quote, I want to compare the plans available for my country, their prices and coverages, and choose one plan that fits my needs.

The plans step uses the active country and validated policyholder and vehicle data from US-01. It displays eligible published plan content in the order configured in Strapi, formats prices for the country, distinguishes a recommended plan, and allows one plan to be chosen for the US-03 summary handoff.

## Scope and dependencies

### In scope

- Read plans for the active country from Strapi and show only plans that are both published and active, in configured order.
- Display each plan's configured name, short description, price, coverages and benefits. Format its price using the country's currency and format.
- Distinguish a recommended plan from the user's selected plan. Recommendation alone does not select a plan.
- Allow exactly one plan selection and keep that selection with the active country's quote so it can be handed to US-03.
- Show an explanatory empty state when no eligible plans exist.
- Provide accessible loading and recoverable error states with retry. Do not show another country's plans or stale plans as current.
- Support keyboard operation and mobile and desktop layouts, consistent with the approved shared design system.

### Dependencies on US-01

- The user must have completed US-01 with a valid form for the country in the URL before entering plans. Invalid or incomplete form data cannot reach plans.
- Returning to US-01 retains its values. Any plan price adjustment that depends on those values must use the current validated data.
- The country URL and country-isolated browser quote state follow approved ADR-001 and ADR-003.

### Out of scope

- US-03 owns the summary content, terms, and payment. US-02 verifies its selection through an observable same-country route or narrow screen handoff seam. The complete quote flow is project-level verification after US-03 exists.
- Real underwriting, rating, or payment services. Use fictitious data and a documented deterministic simulation only if the price question below is resolved in favor of an adjustment.
- Editorial workflows beyond publishing plan content in Strapi.

## Source requirements

| ID | Assessment requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| US02-SR-01 | One application and build serve both countries, and plan changes in Strapi take effect without a code change. | Page 2, scope rules |
| US02-SR-02 | Plan name, short description, base price, currency, coverages, benefits, order, recommended flag, active status and country are managed in Strapi. | Page 7, business rules |
| US02-SR-03 | Show only published, active plans for the current country. | Page 7, business rules |
| US02-SR-04 | Show price in the country's currency and format: Colombian pesos or Chilean pesos. | Page 7, business rules |
| US02-SR-05 | A final price may use a simulated rule based on US-01 data, and that rule is documented. | Page 7, business rules |
| US02-SR-06 | Only one plan can be selected. | Page 7, business rules |
| US02-SR-07 | Show the country's eligible plans in configured order. | Page 7, acceptance scenario “Plans for the country” |
| US02-SR-08 | Visually distinguish a plan marked recommended. | Page 7, acceptance scenario “Recommended plan” |
| US02-SR-09 | Selecting a plan marks it chosen and allows progression to the summary. | Page 7, acceptance scenario “Plan selection” |
| US02-SR-10 | When no active plans exist for the country, explain that no plans are available. | Page 7, acceptance scenario “No plans available” |
| US02-SR-11 | The wizard supports keyboard use, accessible labels, mobile and desktop layouts. | Page 3, accessibility and responsive requirements |

## Functional acceptance criteria

### AC-US02-01 — Country eligibility and configured order

**Given** valid US-01 data exists for the country in the URL and Strapi contains plans for both countries, including draft or inactive plans  
**When** the user opens the plans step  
**Then** only published, active plans for that country are shown  
**And** they appear in their configured order  
**And** a plan change published in Strapi is reflected after the plans content is reloaded without a frontend code change or redeployment.

### AC-US02-02 — Plan details and price

**Given** eligible plans are configured for the active country  
**When** the user compares plans  
**Then** each plan shows its configured name, short description, coverages, and benefits  
**And** its price is shown using the country's currency and format  
**And** the displayed final price follows the resolved pricing rule in Q-US02-01.

### AC-US02-03 — Recommendation and chosen state

**Given** one eligible plan is marked recommended  
**When** the user views the plans  
**Then** that plan is visually identified as recommended  
**And** recommendation is distinguishable from the user's chosen state  
**And** no plan is selected solely because it is recommended.

### AC-US02-04 — Single plan selection and handoff

**Given** the user is viewing eligible plans  
**When** the user chooses a plan  
**Then** that plan is identified as chosen  
**And** choosing another plan replaces the prior choice so only one remains chosen  
**And** the chosen plan and its displayed final price are available to the active country's quote state  
**And** Continue is available only when plan content is ready and the user has explicitly selected a currently eligible plan with a current price based on the current valid US-01 data  
**And** before the first explicit choice, while content is loading or unavailable, or while eligibility and price are being revalidated, the user cannot continue  
**And** a same-country route or narrow screen seam makes the US-03 handoff observable  
**And** US-03 owns the summary content.

### AC-US02-05 — No eligible plans

**Given** the country has no published active plans  
**When** the user opens the plans step  
**Then** an explanatory empty state is shown  
**And** no plan can be selected or submitted  
**And** the user can return to US-01.

### AC-US02-06 — Loading and retrieval failure

**Given** plan content is loading or the request fails  
**When** the plans step is opened or retried  
**Then** an accessible loading status or recoverable error with retry is shown, as applicable  
**And** the user cannot continue without an eligible selected plan  
**And** data and selection are not read from another country's quote  
**And** failed or superseded content is not presented as current  
**And** a refresh, unavailable response, changed US-01 data, or changed plan catalog cannot allow a stale price or an ineligible choice to proceed  
**And** the exact restoration or invalidation policy for a still-eligible selection is defined at the architecture checkpoint.

### AC-US02-07 — Keyboard and responsive use

**Given** the plans step is used on mobile or desktop  
**When** the user navigates and selects using only the keyboard  
**Then** every plan choice has an accessible name and selected state  
**And** the recommendation and price are available with that choice  
**And** the step remains usable at both viewport sizes.

## Proposed tests

| Test ID | Level | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| T-US02-01 | Integration/component | With CO and CL plans, drafts, and inactive plans, verify country filtering, active and published filtering, configured ordering, and pickup of a published change without frontend redeployment. |
| T-US02-02 | Unit/component | Verify configured plan content, country currency formatting, and base price. If an adjustment is approved, verify its deterministic formula, inputs, final price, and rounding behavior. |
| T-US02-03 | Component/accessibility | Verify recommendation is visibly and accessibly distinguished, is not preselected, and remains independent from chosen state. |
| T-US02-04 | Component/integration | Verify plans are rejected until US-01 data is valid, Back returns to the same-country US-01 form with its values retained, one plan can be explicitly selected at a time, Continue is unavailable before that choice, and a same-country route or narrow screen seam exposes the US-03 handoff. |
| T-US02-05 | Component | With no published active plans for the current country, verify the explanatory empty state, blocked progression, and return to US-01. |
| T-US02-06 | Component | Verify loading, request failure, retry, blocked progression, no stale content or price, revalidation after US-01 data or catalog changes, rejection of an ineligible selection, and country isolation. |
| T-US02-07 | Component/accessibility | Navigate and choose plans using only the keyboard at mobile and desktop sizes; verify accessible names and selected/recommended status. |

The full quote flow through summary and payment is deferred to project-level verification after US-03 exists. US-02 verification covers its list, selection, country boundary, and US-03 handoff.

## Existing architecture and implementation seam

- Approved ADR-001 defines the URL country boundary, Strapi published-content read boundary, and a future country-specific Plan collection. It leaves the exact plan shape, public read action, and price rules to this story's architecture stage.
- Approved ADR-003 assigns quote state to the frontend and anticipates a single selected plan reference plus a calculated price snapshot. It leaves selection invalidation and price snapshot details to later rules.
- ADR-002 defines the US-01 form contract. It does not define the plan DTO or runtime validation contract.
- The approved design system and plan concept wireframes specify a native radio choice, separate recommended and selected indicators, and nearby price, coverage, and benefit content. See `docs/design/US-01-design-system.md` and `docs/design/US-01-wireframes.md`.
- The current Angular route and quote state support the US-01 handoff to `/plans`, but the plans view is still a placeholder. No plan collection, plan read endpoint, plan DTO, or plan selection state exists yet.

### Architecture items for the next checkpoint

The approved decisions give direction but not a complete plan contract. After this specification is approved, the architect should define the Strapi Plan schema and public read projection, country and publication filtering, order and stable plan identity, bounded runtime validation and error codes, and how the selection and price snapshot integrate with ADR-003. The architect should decide whether this belongs in a new ADR or an amendment to ADR-001/ADR-003. The approved public-read boundary still applies: no browser write token and only the minimum public read permission.

## Question and proposal

| ID | Status | Question or proposal |
|---|---|---|
| Q-US02-01 | Resolved by Draft 1 approval | The assessment permits a simulated final-price adjustment based on US-01 data but gives no inputs, formula, rounding rule, or display explanation. Is an adjustment required for this increment? **Proposal:** use base price as final price unless a deterministic rule is explicitly approved. If adjustment is required, specify its inputs, formula, rounding, and any explanation shown with the price before approval. |

## Boundaries

- **Always:** Use only the active country's published, active Strapi plans; display the configured order and country currency; keep quote and plan selection in frontend country-scoped state; use fictitious data; preserve accessible keyboard and responsive behavior.
- **Ask first:** Change the approved country or quote-state boundaries, add a dependency, or change this approved specification or a later approved architecture decision.
- **Never:** Expose a Strapi write-privileged token in the browser, use real customer/payment data, or integrate real rating or payment services.

# Spec-Driven Development

## Overview

Write a structured specification before writing any code. The spec is the shared source of truth between you and the human engineer — it defines what we're building, why, and how we'll know it's done. Code without a spec is guessing.

## When to Use

- Starting a new project or feature
- Requirements are ambiguous or incomplete
- The change touches multiple files or modules
- You're about to make an architectural decision
- The task would take more than 30 minutes to implement

**When NOT to use:** Single-line fixes, typo corrections, or changes where requirements are unambiguous and self-contained.

## The Gated Workflow

Spec-driven development has four phases, preceded by a scope check (Phase 0) that activates only when one request bundles several independently testable capabilities. Do not advance to the next phase until the current one is validated.

```
SPECIFY ──→ PLAN ──→ TASKS ──→ IMPLEMENT
   │          │        │          │
   ▼          ▼        ▼          ▼
 Human      Human    Human      Human
 reviews    reviews  reviews    reviews
```

### Phase 0: Scope Check

Most requests describe one capability. If this one does, skip this phase and go straight to Specify — Phase 0 exists for the exception, not the rule, and it puts no hierarchy on single-capability features.

**Detection.** Decompose before specifying when a single requirement bundles several independently testable capabilities:

- The requirement names distinct capabilities with their own consumers or data (e.g. identity, billing, notifications, reporting)
- Acceptance criteria cluster into groups that could ship and be verified separately
- One capability could be cut or replaced without rewriting the others' requirements

**Propose a capability map before writing any spec.** Small and reviewable — a module table plus a build order, not a project plan:

```markdown
# Capability Map: [Initiative Name]

| Module id | Responsibility | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| identity | Accounts, sessions, SSO | — |
| billing | Plans, invoices, payments | identity |
| notifications | Email and webhook fan-out | identity |
| reporting | Usage dashboards | billing, notifications |

Build order: identity → billing, notifications → reporting
```

- **Stable module ids.** Kebab-case, chosen once, never renamed mid-initiative. Specs, plans, and downstream commands select work by these ids instead of guessing which spec is active.
- **Dependency direction, no cycles.** Arrows point one way. If two modules each need the other, they are one module.
- **Interfaces live at the boundary.** The map records that `billing` depends on `identity`; the contract between them belongs in the provider module's spec (see `api-and-interface-design` for designing it).

**The map is gated like every phase.** The human reviews module boundaries, dependency direction, and build order before any module spec is written. Getting the map wrong is expensive; reviewing ten lines is not.

**Then recurse per module.** Run Specify → Plan → Tasks → Implement for each module in dependency order. Each module gets its own spec, scoped to that module's objective, boundaries, and success criteria. Save the approved map as `spec/capability-map.md` and each module's spec alongside it in `spec/`, named by module id (`spec/SPEC-identity.md`, `spec/SPEC-billing.md`) — `/build` already accepts specs under `spec/`, and the root stays uncluttered — the map, not filename guessing, is the index of what exists.

### Phase 1: Specify

Start with a high-level vision. Ask the human clarifying questions until requirements are concrete.

**Surface assumptions immediately.** Before writing any spec content, list what you're assuming:

```
ASSUMPTIONS I'M MAKING:
1. This is a web application (not native mobile)
2. Authentication uses session-based cookies (not JWT)
3. The database is PostgreSQL (based on existing Prisma schema)
4. We're targeting modern browsers only (no IE11)
→ Correct me now or I'll proceed with these.
```

Don't silently fill in ambiguous requirements. The spec's entire purpose is to surface misunderstandings *before* code gets written — assumptions are the most dangerous form of misunderstanding.

**Write a spec document covering these six core areas:**

1. **Objective** — What are we building and why? Who is the user? What does success look like?

2. **Commands** — Full executable commands with flags, not just tool names.
   ```
   Build: npm run build
   Test: npm test -- --coverage
   Lint: npm run lint -- --fix
   Dev: npm run dev
   ```

3. **Project Structure** — Where source code lives, where tests go, where docs belong.
   ```
   src/           → Application source code
   src/components → React components
   src/lib        → Shared utilities
   tests/         → Unit and integration tests
   e2e/           → End-to-end tests
   docs/          → Documentation
   ```

4. **Code Style** — One real code snippet showing your style beats three paragraphs describing it. Include naming conventions, formatting rules, and examples of good output.

5. **Testing Strategy** — What framework, where tests live, coverage expectations, which test levels for which concerns.

6. **Boundaries** — Three-tier system:
   - **Always do:** Run tests before commits, follow naming conventions, validate inputs
   - **Ask first:** Database schema changes, adding dependencies, changing CI config
   - **Never do:** Commit secrets, edit vendor directories, remove failing tests without approval

**Spec template:**

```markdown
# Spec: [Project/Feature Name] — V[N]

## Objective
[What we're building and why. User stories or acceptance criteria.]

## Tech Stack
[Framework, language, key dependencies with versions]

## Commands
[Build, test, lint, dev — full commands]

## Project Structure
[Directory layout with descriptions]

## Code Style
[Example snippet + key conventions]

## Testing Strategy
[Framework, test locations, coverage requirements, test levels]

## Boundaries
- Always: [...]
- Ask first: [...]
- Never: [...]

## Success Criteria
[How we'll know this is done — specific, testable conditions]

## Out of Scope (Deferred)
[Ideas explicitly excluded from this version — the V2 backlog. One line each: what, and why it's deferred.]

## Open Questions
[Anything unresolved that needs human input]
```

**External spec tools:** This workflow is format-agnostic. If the project
already uses OpenSpec or another specification system, keep that system's
artifact format and storage conventions instead of creating a duplicate
`SPEC.md`. This skill owns the clarification, content, and approval gates; the
external tool owns how the approved spec is represented.

**Reframe instructions as success criteria.** When receiving vague requirements, translate them into concrete conditions:

```
REQUIREMENT: "Make the dashboard faster"

REFRAMED SUCCESS CRITERIA:
- Dashboard LCP < 2.5s on 4G connection
- Initial data load completes in < 500ms
- No layout shift during load (CLS < 0.1)
→ Are these the right targets?
```

This lets you loop, retry, and problem-solve toward a clear goal rather than guessing what "faster" means.

**Stop after writing the spec (CRITICAL).** Once the spec is saved:

1. Summarize it and list any Open Questions.
2. Ask the human to approve it or request changes.
3. **STOP YOUR TURN IMMEDIATELY.** Do NOT start Phase 2, invoke `planning-and-task-breakdown`, or write code in this turn. Planning starts only after the human approves the spec in a later turn.

### Phase 2: Plan

With the validated spec, generate a technical implementation plan:

1. Identify the major components and their dependencies
2. Determine the implementation order (what must be built first)
3. Note risks and mitigation strategies
4. Identify what can be built in parallel vs. what must be sequential
5. Define verification checkpoints between phases

> Follow `planning-and-task-breakdown` for the dependency-graph mapping and vertical-slicing mechanics behind these steps; it is the canonical source. The bullets above are a lightweight summary; if they ever diverge, `planning-and-task-breakdown` takes precedence.
>
> **Output convention:** Save the plan to `tasks/plan.md` and record the task list in the task list target defined by `planning-and-task-breakdown` (default `tasks/todo.md`; projects may designate an external tracker instead). Create `tasks/` if it does not exist. Downstream commands (`/build`, etc.) expect these defaults.

The plan should be reviewable: the human should be able to read it and say "yes, that's the right approach" or "no, change X."

### Phase 3: Tasks

Break the plan into discrete, implementable tasks:

- Each task should be completable in a single focused session
- Each task has explicit acceptance criteria
- Each task includes a verification step (test, build, manual check)
- Tasks are ordered by dependency, not by perceived importance
- No task should require changing more than ~5 files

> Follow `planning-and-task-breakdown` for the full task-sizing and dependency-ordering mechanics; it is the canonical source. The template below is a lightweight inline form; if they ever diverge, `planning-and-task-breakdown` takes precedence.

**Task template:**
```markdown
- [ ] Task: [Description]
  - Acceptance: [What must be true when done]
  - Verify: [How to confirm — test command, build, manual check]
  - Files: [Which files will be touched]
```

### Phase 4: Implement

Execute tasks one at a time following `skills/incremental-implementation/SKILL.md` (`incremental-implementation`) and `skills/test-driven-development/SKILL.md` (`test-driven-development`). Use `skills/context-engineering/SKILL.md` (`context-engineering`) to load the right spec sections and source files at each step rather than flooding the agent with the entire spec.

## Keeping the Spec Alive

The spec is a living document, not a one-time artifact:

- **Update when decisions change** — If you discover the data model needs to change, update the spec first, then implement.
- **Update when scope changes** — Features added or cut should be reflected in the spec.
- **Commit the spec** — The spec belongs in version control alongside the code.
- **Reference the spec in PRs** — Link back to the spec section that each PR implements.

## Spec Evolution: V1 Scoping and Follow-Up Changes

A spec describes one version of the work. New ideas and post-ship changes don't expand it — they queue behind it.

### Scope each version explicitly

Label the spec with the version it describes, in the title (`# Spec: Invoice Pipeline — V1`). When a shipped delta is folded back in, bump the version — the label always states which version of the system the spec describes, and makes "that's a V2 idea" an objective call rather than a judgment made mid-build.

During Specify, ideas that won't make this version go under **Out of Scope (Deferred)** — captured, not lost. This makes the V1 boundary enforceable: during implementation, anything not in the spec's requirements is out, even if it's written in the same file under Deferred. When an idea arrives mid-build, park it in the Deferred list and keep going; re-scoping happens between versions, not during one.

### Follow-up changes get a delta spec

Once a spec has shipped, a new requirement — swapping the storage engine, replacing a manual step with OCR, promoting a deferred V2 item — gets its own small spec rather than a hand-edit of the shipped one. A delta spec covers only what changes:

```markdown
# Spec Delta: [Change Name]

Status: proposed

## Objective
[The change and why. Which deferred item or new requirement this implements.]

## Current Behavior
[What exists today — link the relevant section of the original spec.]

## New Behavior
[What will be true after the change.]

## Success Criteria
[Specific, testable conditions — including what must NOT change.]

## Boundaries
[Only deltas from the original spec's boundaries; everything else inherits.]
```

Save it alongside the original (e.g. `SPEC-postgres-migration.md` next to `SPEC.md`) and run it through the same gated workflow: human review, then plan, tasks, implement. Downstream commands know this convention — `/build auto` accepts a root-level `SPEC-<change>.md` as the spec for a follow-up change and treats it as a planning artifact in its clean-baseline check. Keep one change per delta spec — that keeps each plan/build cycle small and reviewable.

After the change ships, fold the outcome into the original spec (per Keeping the Spec Alive) so it stays the source of truth for what exists, and mark the delta implemented by changing its `Status:` line to `Status: implemented`. The original spec always describes the current system; delta specs describe transitions.

## Common Rationalizations

| Rationalization | Reality |
|---|---|
| "This is simple, I don't need a spec" | Simple tasks don't need *long* specs, but they still need acceptance criteria. A two-line spec is fine. |
| "I'll write the spec after I code it" | That's documentation, not specification. The spec's value is in forcing clarity *before* code. |
| "The spec will slow us down" | A 15-minute spec prevents hours of rework. Waterfall in 15 minutes beats debugging in 15 hours. |
| "Requirements will change anyway" | That's why the spec is a living document. An outdated spec is still better than no spec. |
| "The user knows what they want" | Even clear requests have implicit assumptions. The spec surfaces those assumptions. |
| "This idea is good, I'll fold it into the current spec" | Mid-build scope growth is how V1 slips. Park it under Out of Scope (Deferred) — captured without expanding the current cycle. |
| "The feature already has a spec, I'll just edit it for the change" | A shipped spec describes what exists. A delta spec keeps the change reviewable on its own; the original gets updated after the change ships, not before. |
| "It's one big feature; splitting it is overhead" | If acceptance criteria cluster into independently testable groups, a monolithic spec forces every downstream task to reason over the whole contract. A ten-line capability map is the cheap alternative. |
| "I'll decompose during planning" | Planning slices tasks within a spec. By then the oversized artifact already exists — module boundaries and dependency direction must be decided before the spec is written, not after. |

## Red Flags

- Starting to write code without any written requirements
- Asking "should I just start building?" before clarifying what "done" means
- Implementing features not mentioned in any spec or task list
- Making architectural decisions without documenting them
- Skipping the spec because "it's obvious what to build"
- V1 requirements growing mid-implementation as new ideas get written straight into the spec
- Changing a shipped feature with no spec for the change because "the feature already has one"
- Writing the spec and starting the plan or code in the same turn
- One spec whose requirements span several independently testable capabilities
- Module boundaries or build order decided implicitly during implementation because no capability map was approved up front

## Verification

Before proceeding to implementation, confirm:

- [ ] The spec covers all six core areas (a full spec; a delta spec covers only the areas the change affects — at minimum objective, success criteria, and boundary deltas — and inherits the rest from the original)
- [ ] The human has reviewed and approved the spec
- [ ] The turn ended after saving the spec; approval came in a later turn
- [ ] Success criteria are specific and testable
- [ ] Boundaries (Always/Ask First/Never) are defined
- [ ] The spec is saved to a file in the repository
- [ ] Ideas cut from this version are captured under Out of Scope (Deferred), not silently dropped or silently included
- [ ] If this is a change to a shipped spec, it is a delta spec referencing the original, not a rewrite of it
- [ ] If the request bundles several independently testable capabilities, a capability map (module ids, dependency direction, build order) was approved before any module spec was written
- [ ] Every module spec traces to a module id in the approved map

# Angular Developer Guidelines

1. Always analyze the project's Angular version before providing guidance, as best practices and available features can vary significantly between versions. If creating a new project with Angular CLI, do not specify a version unless prompted by the user.

2. When generating code, follow Angular's style guide and best practices for maintainability and performance. Use the Angular CLI for scaffolding components, services, directives, pipes, and routes to ensure consistency.

**Step 3: Fallback to Latest.**

name: spec-driven-development
description: Creates specs before coding. Use when starting a new project, feature, or significant change and no specification exists yet. Use when drafting a PRD or requirements document with objectives and scope, or when requirements are unclear, ambiguous, or only exist as a vague idea. Use when a single requirement spans several independently testable capabilities and needs decomposing into a capability map of modules before specifying. Use when evolving a shipped spec — scoping a V1, deferring ideas to a V2 backlog, or writing a follow-up spec for a change to an existing feature.
---

# Spec-Driven Development

## Overview

Write a structured specification before writing any code. The spec is the shared source of truth between you and the human engineer — it defines what we're building, why, and how we'll know it's done. Code without a spec is guessing.

## When to Use

- Starting a new project or feature
- Requirements are ambiguous or incomplete
- The change touches multiple files or modules
- You're about to make an architectural decision
- The task would take more than 30 minutes to implement

**When NOT to use:** Single-line fixes, typo corrections, or changes where requirements are unambiguous and self-contained.

## The Gated Workflow

Spec-driven development has four phases, preceded by a scope check (Phase 0) that activates only when one request bundles several independently testable capabilities. Do not advance to the next phase until the current one is validated.

```
SPECIFY ──→ PLAN ──→ TASKS ──→ IMPLEMENT
   │          │        │          │
   ▼          ▼        ▼          ▼
 Human      Human    Human      Human
 reviews    reviews  reviews    reviews
```

### Phase 0: Scope Check

Most requests describe one capability. If this one does, skip this phase and go straight to Specify — Phase 0 exists for the exception, not the rule, and it puts no hierarchy on single-capability features.

**Detection.** Decompose before specifying when a single requirement bundles several independently testable capabilities:

- The requirement names distinct capabilities with their own consumers or data (e.g. identity, billing, notifications, reporting)
- Acceptance criteria cluster into groups that could ship and be verified separately
- One capability could be cut or replaced without rewriting the others' requirements

**Propose a capability map before writing any spec.** Small and reviewable — a module table plus a build order, not a project plan:

```markdown
# Capability Map: [Initiative Name]

| Module id | Responsibility | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| identity | Accounts, sessions, SSO | — |
| billing | Plans, invoices, payments | identity |
| notifications | Email and webhook fan-out | identity |
| reporting | Usage dashboards | billing, notifications |

Build order: identity → billing, notifications → reporting
```

- **Stable module ids.** Kebab-case, chosen once, never renamed mid-initiative. Specs, plans, and downstream commands select work by these ids instead of guessing which spec is active.
- **Dependency direction, no cycles.** Arrows point one way. If two modules each need the other, they are one module.
- **Interfaces live at the boundary.** The map records that `billing` depends on `identity`; the contract between them belongs in the provider module's spec (see `api-and-interface-design` for designing it).

**The map is gated like every phase.** The human reviews module boundaries, dependency direction, and build order before any module spec is written. Getting the map wrong is expensive; reviewing ten lines is not.

**Then recurse per module.** Run Specify → Plan → Tasks → Implement for each module in dependency order. Each module gets its own spec, scoped to that module's objective, boundaries, and success criteria. Save the approved map as `spec/capability-map.md` and each module's spec alongside it in `spec/`, named by module id (`spec/SPEC-identity.md`, `spec/SPEC-billing.md`) — `/build` already accepts specs under `spec/`, and the root stays uncluttered — the map, not filename guessing, is the index of what exists.

### Phase 1: Specify

Start with a high-level vision. Ask the human clarifying questions until requirements are concrete.

**Surface assumptions immediately.** Before writing any spec content, list what you're assuming:

```
ASSUMPTIONS I'M MAKING:
1. This is a web application (not native mobile)
2. Authentication uses session-based cookies (not JWT)
3. The database is PostgreSQL (based on existing Prisma schema)
4. We're targeting modern browsers only (no IE11)
→ Correct me now or I'll proceed with these.
```

Don't silently fill in ambiguous requirements. The spec's entire purpose is to surface misunderstandings *before* code gets written — assumptions are the most dangerous form of misunderstanding.

**Write a spec document covering these six core areas:**

1. **Objective** — What are we building and why? Who is the user? What does success look like?

2. **Commands** — Full executable commands with flags, not just tool names.
   ```
   Build: npm run build
   Test: npm test -- --coverage
   Lint: npm run lint -- --fix
   Dev: npm run dev
   ```

3. **Project Structure** — Where source code lives, where tests go, where docs belong.
   ```
   src/           → Application source code
   src/components → React components
   src/lib        → Shared utilities
   tests/         → Unit and integration tests
   e2e/           → End-to-end tests
   docs/          → Documentation
   ```

4. **Code Style** — One real code snippet showing your style beats three paragraphs describing it. Include naming conventions, formatting rules, and examples of good output.

5. **Testing Strategy** — What framework, where tests live, coverage expectations, which test levels for which concerns.

6. **Boundaries** — Three-tier system:
   - **Always do:** Run tests before commits, follow naming conventions, validate inputs
   - **Ask first:** Database schema changes, adding dependencies, changing CI config
   - **Never do:** Commit secrets, edit vendor directories, remove failing tests without approval

**Spec template:**

```markdown
# Spec: [Project/Feature Name] — V[N]

## Objective
[What we're building and why. User stories or acceptance criteria.]

## Tech Stack
[Framework, language, key dependencies with versions]

## Commands
[Build, test, lint, dev — full commands]

## Project Structure
[Directory layout with descriptions]

## Code Style
[Example snippet + key conventions]

## Testing Strategy
[Framework, test locations, coverage requirements, test levels]

## Boundaries
- Always: [...]
- Ask first: [...]
- Never: [...]

## Success Criteria
[How we'll know this is done — specific, testable conditions]

## Out of Scope (Deferred)
[Ideas explicitly excluded from this version — the V2 backlog. One line each: what, and why it's deferred.]

## Open Questions
[Anything unresolved that needs human input]
```

**External spec tools:** This workflow is format-agnostic. If the project
already uses OpenSpec or another specification system, keep that system's
artifact format and storage conventions instead of creating a duplicate
`SPEC.md`. This skill owns the clarification, content, and approval gates; the
external tool owns how the approved spec is represented.

**Reframe instructions as success criteria.** When receiving vague requirements, translate them into concrete conditions:

```
REQUIREMENT: "Make the dashboard faster"

REFRAMED SUCCESS CRITERIA:
- Dashboard LCP < 2.5s on 4G connection
- Initial data load completes in < 500ms
- No layout shift during load (CLS < 0.1)
→ Are these the right targets?
```

This lets you loop, retry, and problem-solve toward a clear goal rather than guessing what "faster" means.

**Stop after writing the spec (CRITICAL).** Once the spec is saved:

1. Summarize it and list any Open Questions.
2. Ask the human to approve it or request changes.
3. **STOP YOUR TURN IMMEDIATELY.** Do NOT start Phase 2, invoke `planning-and-task-breakdown`, or write code in this turn. Planning starts only after the human approves the spec in a later turn.

### Phase 2: Plan

With the validated spec, generate a technical implementation plan:

1. Identify the major components and their dependencies
2. Determine the implementation order (what must be built first)
3. Note risks and mitigation strategies
4. Identify what can be built in parallel vs. what must be sequential
5. Define verification checkpoints between phases

> Follow `planning-and-task-breakdown` for the dependency-graph mapping and vertical-slicing mechanics behind these steps; it is the canonical source. The bullets above are a lightweight summary; if they ever diverge, `planning-and-task-breakdown` takes precedence.
>
> **Output convention:** Save the plan to `tasks/plan.md` and record the task list in the task list target defined by `planning-and-task-breakdown` (default `tasks/todo.md`; projects may designate an external tracker instead). Create `tasks/` if it does not exist. Downstream commands (`/build`, etc.) expect these defaults.

The plan should be reviewable: the human should be able to read it and say "yes, that's the right approach" or "no, change X."

### Phase 3: Tasks

Break the plan into discrete, implementable tasks:

- Each task should be completable in a single focused session
- Each task has explicit acceptance criteria
- Each task includes a verification step (test, build, manual check)
- Tasks are ordered by dependency, not by perceived importance
- No task should require changing more than ~5 files

> Follow `planning-and-task-breakdown` for the full task-sizing and dependency-ordering mechanics; it is the canonical source. The template below is a lightweight inline form; if they ever diverge, `planning-and-task-breakdown` takes precedence.

**Task template:**
```markdown
- [ ] Task: [Description]
  - Acceptance: [What must be true when done]
  - Verify: [How to confirm — test command, build, manual check]
  - Files: [Which files will be touched]
```

### Phase 4: Implement

Execute tasks one at a time following `skills/incremental-implementation/SKILL.md` (`incremental-implementation`) and `skills/test-driven-development/SKILL.md` (`test-driven-development`). Use `skills/context-engineering/SKILL.md` (`context-engineering`) to load the right spec sections and source files at each step rather than flooding the agent with the entire spec.

## Keeping the Spec Alive

The spec is a living document, not a one-time artifact:

- **Update when decisions change** — If you discover the data model needs to change, update the spec first, then implement.
- **Update when scope changes** — Features added or cut should be reflected in the spec.
- **Commit the spec** — The spec belongs in version control alongside the code.
- **Reference the spec in PRs** — Link back to the spec section that each PR implements.

## Spec Evolution: V1 Scoping and Follow-Up Changes

A spec describes one version of the work. New ideas and post-ship changes don't expand it — they queue behind it.

### Scope each version explicitly

Label the spec with the version it describes, in the title (`# Spec: Invoice Pipeline — V1`). When a shipped delta is folded back in, bump the version — the label always states which version of the system the spec describes, and makes "that's a V2 idea" an objective call rather than a judgment made mid-build.

During Specify, ideas that won't make this version go under **Out of Scope (Deferred)** — captured, not lost. This makes the V1 boundary enforceable: during implementation, anything not in the spec's requirements is out, even if it's written in the same file under Deferred. # Angular Developer Guidelines

1. Always analyze the project's Angular version before providing guidance, as best practices and available features can vary significantly between versions. If creating a new project with Angular CLI, do not specify a version unless prompted by the user.

2. When generating code, follow Angular's style guide and best practices for maintainability and performance. Use the Angular CLI for scaffolding components, services, directives, pipes, and routes to ensure consistency.

3. Once you finish generating code, run `ng build` to ensure there are no build errors. If there are errors, analyze the error messages and fix them before proceeding. Do not skip this step, as it is critical for ensuring the generated code is correct and functional.

## Creating New Projects

If no guidelines are provided by the user, here are some default rules to follow when creating a new Angular project:

1. Use the latest stable version of Angular unless the user specifies otherwise.
2. Use Signal Forms for form management in new projects (stable in Angular v22 and newer) [Find out more](references/signal-forms.md).

**Execution Rules for `ng new`:**
When asked to create a new Angular project, you must determine the correct execution command by following these strict steps:

**Step 1: Check for an explicit user version.**

- **IF** the user requests a specific version (e.g., Angular 15), bypass local installations and strictly use `npx`.
- **Command:** `npx @angular/cli@<requested_version> new <project-name>`

**Step 2: Check for an existing Angular installation.**

- **IF** no specific version is requested, run `ng version` in the terminal to check if the Angular CLI is already installed on the system.
- **IF** the command succeeds and returns an installed version, use the local/global installation directly.
- **Command:** `ng new <project-name>`

**Step 3: Fallback to Latest.**

- **IF** no specific version is requested AND the `ng version` command fails (indicating no Angular installation exists), you must use `npx` to fetch the latest version.
- **Command:** `npx @angular/cli@latest new <project-name>`

## Components

When working with Angular components, consult the following references based on the task:

- **Fundamentals**: Anatomy, metadata, core concepts, self-closing tags, and template control flow (@if, @for, @switch). Read [components.md](references/components.md)
- **Inputs**: Signal-based inputs, transforms, and model inputs. Read [inputs.md](references/inputs.md)
- **Outputs**: Signal-based outputs and custom event best practices. Read [outputs.md](references/outputs.md)
- **Host Elements**: Host bindings and attribute injection. Read [host-elements.md](references/host-elements.md)
- **Naming Conventions**: Modern Angular v20+ naming style ("Intent over Role") for files, components, services, directives, pipes, and models. Read [naming-conventions.md](references/naming-conventions.md)
- **Queries and Content Projection**: Signal-based view and content queries (viewChild, viewChildren, contentChild, contentChildren) and content projection with `<ng-content>` slots and fallback content. Read [queries-and-projection.md](references/queries-and-projection.md)
- **Deferrable Views**: Lazy loading, code splitting, triggers, prefetching, loading states, SSR, and layout stability with `@defer`. Read [deferrable-views.md](references/deferrable-views.md)
- **Error Boundaries**: Catching render and change detection errors in a template subtree with `@boundary`/`@error`, retrying with `$reset`. Read [error-boundary.md](references/error-boundary.md)

**Template expressions**: Avoid expensive work in templates (e.g. building arrays or objects, filtering, sorting), since it re-runs on every change detection cycle. Reading signals (`count()`) and cheap calls are fine. Derive other values with `computed()`, a pure pipe, or a child component. See [Avoiding expensive work in templates](references/components.md#avoiding-expensive-work-in-templates).

If you require deeper documentation not found in the references above, read the documentation at `https://angular.dev/guide/components`.

### In scope

- Read plans for the active country from Strapi and show only plans that are both published and active, in configured order.
- Display each plan's configured name, short description, price, coverages and benefits. Format its price using the country's currency and format.
- Distinguish a recommended plan from the user's selected plan. Recommendation alone does not select a plan.
- Allow exactly one plan selection and keep that selection with the active country's quote so it can be handed to US-03.
- Show an explanatory empty state when no eligible plans exist.
- Provide accessible loading and recoverable error states with retry. Do not show another country's plans or stale plans as current.
- Support keyboard operation and mobile and desktop layouts, consistent with the approved shared design system.

### Dependencies on US-01

- The user must have completed US-01 with a valid form for the country in the URL before entering plans. Invalid or incomplete form data cannot reach plans.
- Returning to US-01 retains its values. Any plan price adjustment that depends on those values must use the current validated data.
- The country URL and country-isolated browser quote state follow approved ADR-001 and ADR-003.

### Out of scope

- US-03 owns the summary content, terms, and payment. US-02 verifies its selection through an observable same-country route or narrow screen handoff seam. The complete quote flow is project-level verification after US-03 exists.
- Real underwriting, rating, or payment services. Use fictitious data and a documented deterministic simulation only if the price question below is resolved in favor of an adjustment.
- Editorial workflows beyond publishing plan content in Strapi.

| US02-SR-05 | A final price may use a simulated rule based on US-01 data, and that rule is documented. | Page 7, business rules |
| US02-SR-06 | Only one plan can be selected. | Page 7, business rules |
| US02-SR-07 | Show the country's eligible plans in configured order. | Page 7, acceptance scenario “Plans for the country” |
| US02-SR-08 | Visually distinguish a plan marked recommended. | Page 7, acceptance scenario “Recommended plan” |
| US02-SR-09 | Selecting a plan marks it chosen and allows progression to the summary. | Page 7, acceptance scenario “Plan selection” |
| US02-SR-10 | When no active plans exist for the country, explain that no plans are available. | Page 7, acceptance scenario “No plans available” |
| US02-SR-11 | The wizard supports keyboard use, accessible labels, mobile and desktop layouts. | Page 3, accessibility and responsive requirements |

## Functional acceptance criteria

### AC-US02-01 — Country eligibility and configured order

**Given** valid US-01 data exists for the country in the URL and Strapi contains plans for both countries, including draft or inactive plans  
**When** the user opens the plans step  
**Then** only published, active plans for that country are shown  
**And** they appear in their configured order  
**And** a plan change published in Strapi is reflected after the plans content is reloaded without a frontend code change or redeployment.

### AC-US02-02 — Plan details and price

**Given** eligible plans are configured for the active country  
**When** the user compares plans  
**Then** each plan shows its configured name, short description, coverages, and benefits  
**And** its price is shown using the country's currency and format  
**And** the displayed final price follows the resolved pricing rule in Q-US02-01.

### AC-US02-03 — Recommendation and chosen state

**Given** one eligible plan is marked recommended  
**When** the user views the plans  
**Then** that plan is visually identified as recommended  
**And** recommendation is distinguishable from the user's chosen state  
**And** no plan is selected solely because it is recommended.

### AC-US02-04 — Single plan selection and handoff

**Given** the user is viewing eligible plans  
**When** the user chooses a plan  
**Then** that plan is identified as chosen  
**And** choosing another plan replaces the prior choice so only one remains chosen  
**And** the chosen plan and its displayed final price are available to the active country's quote state  
**And** Continue is available only when plan content is ready and the user has explicitly selected a currently eligible plan with a current price based on the current valid US-01 data  
**And** before the first explicit choice, while content is loading or unavailable, or while eligibility and price are being revalidated, the user cannot continue  
**And** a same-country route or narrow screen seam makes the US-03 handoff observable  
**And** US-03 owns the summary content.

### AC-US02-05 — No eligible plans

**Given** the country has no published active plans  
**When** the user opens the plans step  
**Then** an explanatory empty state is shown  
**And** no plan can be selected or submitted  
**And** the user can return to US-01.

### AC-US02-06 — Loading and retrieval failure

**Given** plan content is loading or the request fails  
**When** the plans step is opened or retried  
**Then** an accessible loading status or recoverable error with retry is shown, as applicable  
**And** the user cannot continue without an eligible selected plan  
**And** data and selection are not read from another country's quote  
**And** failed or superseded content is not presented as current  
**And** a refresh, unavailable response, changed US-01 data, or changed plan catalog cannot allow a stale price or an ineligible choice to proceed  
**And** the exact restoration or invalidation policy for a still-eligible selection is defined at the architecture checkpoint.

### AC-US02-07 — Keyboard and responsive use

**Given** the plans step is used on mobile or desktop  
**When** the user navigates and selects using only the keyboard  
**Then** every plan choice has an accessible name and selected state  
**And** the recommendation and price are available with that choice  
**And** the step remains usable at both viewport sizes.

| Test ID | Level | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| T-US02-01 | Integration/component | With CO and CL plans, drafts, and inactive plans, verify country filtering, active and published filtering, configured ordering, and pickup of a published change without frontend redeployment. |
| T-US02-02 | Unit/component | Verify configured plan content, country currency formatting, and base price. If an adjustment is approved, verify its deterministic formula, inputs, final price, and rounding behavior. |
| T-US02-03 | Component/accessibility | Verify recommendation is visibly and accessibly distinguished, is not preselected, and remains independent from chosen state. |
| T-US02-04 | Component/integration | Verify plans are rejected until US-01 data is valid, Back returns to the same-country US-01 form with its values retained, one plan can be explicitly selected at a time, Continue is unavailable before that choice, and a same-country route or narrow screen seam exposes the US-03 handoff. |
| T-US02-05 | Component | With no published active plans for the current country, verify the explanatory empty state, blocked progression, and return to US-01. |
| T-US02-06 | Component | Verify loading, request failure, retry, blocked progression, no stale content or price, revalidation after US-01 data or catalog changes, rejection of an ineligible selection, and country isolation. |
| T-US02-07 | Component/accessibility | Navigate and choose plans using only the keyboard at mobile and desktop sizes; verify accessible names and selected/recommended status. |

The full quote flow through summary and payment is deferred to project-level verification after US-03 exists. US-02 verification covers its list, selection, country boundary, and US-03 handoff.

## Existing architecture and implementation seam

- Approved ADR-001 defines the URL country boundary, Strapi published-content read boundary, and a future country-specific Plan collection. It leaves the exact plan shape, public read action, and price rules to this story's architecture stage.
- Approved ADR-003 assigns quote state to the frontend and anticipates a single selected plan reference plus a calculated price snapshot. It leaves selection invalidation and price snapshot details to later rules.
- ADR-002 defines the US-01 form contract. It does not define the plan DTO or runtime validation contract.
- The approved design system and plan concept wireframes specify a native radio choice, separate recommended and selected indicators, and nearby price, coverage, and benefit content. See `docs/design/US-01-design-system.md` and `docs/design/US-01-wireframes.md`.
- The current Angular route and quote state support the US-01 handoff to `/plans`, but the plans view is still a placeholder. No plan collection, plan read endpoint, plan DTO, or plan selection state exists yet.

### Architecture items for the next checkpoint

The approved decisions give direction but not a complete plan contract. After this specification is approved, the architect should define the Strapi Plan schema and public read projection, country and publication filtering, order and stable plan identity, bounded runtime validation and error codes, and how the selection and price snapshot integrate with ADR-003. The architect should decide whether this belongs in a new ADR or an amendment to ADR-001/ADR-003. The approved public-read boundary still applies: no browser write token and only the minimum public read permission.

|---|---|---|
| Q-US02-01 | Resolved by Draft 1 approval | The assessment permits a simulated final-price adjustment based on US-01 data but gives no inputs, formula, rounding rule, or display explanation. Is an adjustment required for this increment? **Proposal:** use base price as final price unless a deterministic rule is explicitly approved. If adjustment is required, specify its inputs, formula, rounding, and any explanation shown with the price before approval. |

- **Always:** Use only the active country's published, active Strapi plans; display the configured order and country currency; keep quote and plan selection in frontend country-scoped state; use fictitious data; preserve accessible keyboard and responsive behavior.
- **Ask first:** Change the approved country or quote-state boundaries, add a dependency, or change this approved specification or a later approved architecture decision.
- **Never:** Expose a Strapi write-privileged token in the browser, use real customer/payment data, or integrate real rating or payment services.
